title: The paragraph that is not there: limitations, cost, and the counterexample

what.formal: The **limitations statement** is the part of a paper in which the authors name the conditions under which their claims may fail, the costs of their method, and the questions their experiments do not settle. A **negative result** is a result within the paper's own experiments that contradicts or bounds one of its claims. Section VI of this paper contains neither: it has no limitations paragraph, no computational cost figures, no discussion of the one dataset where the method fails to beat its baseline, and its only forward-looking sentence is "pave the way for future research in this field".
what.plain: There is no paragraph saying what the method cannot do. This card is about that absence — what a limitations paragraph would have had to say, and what it costs a reader that it is not there.

what.md: **Why an absent limitations section is a stronger claim than a weak one.** A short or vague limitations paragraph still tells you the authors looked. Its absence tells you either that they found nothing worth naming — implausible for a method with six hyperparameters, a pre-trained component and a data-dependent hyperedge construction — or that they decided not to say. Those two possibilities lead to very different places, and the paper gives no way to choose between them. In a venue where the section is conventional, the reader is left to do the authors' work.

**The test to apply to your own reading of this, before accepting it.** The absence is real, but its significance depends on the venue's norms, and different fields treat it differently. A TPAMI paper in 2026 is expected to include a limitations discussion; a short conference paper often is not. The check is cheap: open three or four recent papers from the same venue and look for the paragraph. If it is there in most, its absence here is a choice. That is a check any reader can run and no amount of close reading can replace.

example.md: **Walk 1 — the four jobs of a conclusion, and which are done.** The paragraph being assessed is Section VI, whose five sentences name, in order: the framework; the pair of encoders; the fusion module; the two models; and a closing claim about the field. Its words are quoted in full in card 110.

example.md: **The third row is the one that reshapes how the rest of the paper reads.** Every question a reader accumulates while reading — and the last card of this chapter collects six of them — lands in the limitations paragraph when the authors have anticipated it, and nowhere at all when they have not. So a missing limitations paragraph is not a missing apology. It is a missing map of the paper's own uncertainties, which means the reader has to build that map from scratch, using the tables and the arithmetic. Names used throughout: **GBDT** is the gradient-boosted decision tree ensemble; **TDR-Encoder** is the paper's rule encoder (card 68); **HGNN** is the hypergraph neural network whose propagation is the paper's Equation (1); **RD-HGNN** and **DD-HGNN** are the paper's two models, taking the rule stream alone and the rule plus structural streams together (cards 74–75).
**Walk 2 — the limitations a reader can reconstruct, in order of how much they matter.** Each of these is derivable from the paper's own text; none is stated in it.

items.md: Note the shape of the first item: it is not a limitation the authors overlooked. It is one whose *statement* would have resolved a doubt, and whose omission leaves the doubt open.
items.why: This is the category to look for when a limitations section is missing: things the paper could have said in one sentence and did not. A limitation that requires new experiments is excusable; a limitation that requires one clause in Section IV-D is not. That the rule encoder is pre-trained on "predefined tasks" without saying whose labels those tasks use is exactly that kind — and its consequence is the largest of the six, because it bears on every number in the paper.

items.md: The second and third items compound: the method's fixed cost is not reported, and the quantity that most determines it is not reported either.
items.why: Hold those two together and the omission becomes concrete. Table IV lists tree counts running from 20 to 190 and depths up to 7; card 93's bound gives a rule block of up to $C_r \le \text{trees} \times (2^d - 1)$ entries per vertex, doubled by the content-and-position pairing. For Github that reaches into the thousands of columns per vertex, each a real number. **A reader planning to apply the method cannot estimate whether it will fit in memory**, and the paper's only response to the question is a sentence about its own hardware.

items.md: Now the sixth item, which is the mildest and the most instructive about how to read a results table.
items.why: It is a *consistency* observation rather than a missing experiment: MLP and GBDT cannot see the graph, so on three datasets built from the same 2,708 publications they should agree, and they do not for the plain-graph variant. Card 100 worked this through. The reason to put it in a limitations list is not that it undermines a claim — it does not — but that it bounds one: the paper's statements about "Cora" are statements about one of three distinct experimental setups, and its own abstract's headline "$7.3\%$ gain on the Cora dataset" therefore names no experiment: the same comparison comes out at $7.30$ on one of the three and $6.83$ on another.

example.md: **Walk 3 — the negative result that is in the tables and not in the text.** The clearest example is small enough to state in one line: on Github, under the production setting, the paper's models lose to the plain HGNN baseline, by $0.09$ points for the better of the two. Section VI claims "superior performance across diverse datasets". Section V-B states the rule — RD wins on graph datasets, DD on hypergraph datasets — and Github is a graph dataset.

**It is worth being precise about what is and is not objectionable here.** The result itself is unobjectionable: a 0.09-point deficit on one of ten datasets is inside the run-to-run spread, and no reasonable reader would treat it as refuting a method that wins on the other nine. What is missing is one sentence naming it. A paper that said "on Github our models are level with HGNN, which we attribute to the dataset's shallow structure" would be *stronger*, not weaker — the claim would then be bounded and therefore checkable, and the nine wins would read as measured rather than as selected. **The cost of not writing that sentence is not that the paper overstates by 0.09 points. It is that a reader who finds the row must now wonder what else the prose smoothed over.**

Section VI's final sentence — "pave the way for future research in this field" — is the corresponding gap on the forward side. It names no direction. Against the six items above, a future-work list almost writes itself: specify the pre-training label boundary, report ledger widths and timings, rerun the $k$ sweep for hyperedge construction, repeat the ablations on a second dataset, and test what happens when the binarised rule content is replaced by a distance-preserving value. **Each is a concrete experiment, and each is the kind of thing the sentence "paves the way" was standing in front of.**

quiz.q: Why is the *absence* of a limitations section more informative than a brief one would have been?

opts.md: Because it proves the authors did not consider any limitations
opts.expl: It proves nothing of the kind. It may equally mean the authors considered several and chose not to write them, which is the more common situation in a paper whose method has six hyperparameters and a pre-trained component. The point is that the absence leaves the reader unable to distinguish those cases.

opts.md: Because it removes the reader's map of the paper's own uncertainties, leaving them to reconstruct it from the tables
opts.expl: Correct. A limitations paragraph is where anticipated doubts are collected and addressed. Without it, each doubt has to be rediscovered independently — which is exactly what the published commentary on a paper does, and what this site's critique chapter is doing with arithmetic instead. Notice that the reconstruction is possible here; the six items in Walk 2 all come from the paper's own text. It is the *labour* that has been moved to the reader, not the information.

opts.md: Because a limitations section is required by the venue's submission guidelines
opts.expl: Venue norms are a real consideration and a check any reader can run in five minutes by opening recent papers from the same venue. But a formatting lapse is a much weaker finding than a missing map of uncertainties, and stating the weaker version would overstate what the absence shows.

quiz.q: The card lists six limitations a reader can reconstruct from the paper's own text. Which of them cannot be closed by any further reading, further data, or further experiment carried out by a third party?

opts.expl: A third party can time the method on their own hardware. Cost is a measurement, and the paper's omission makes it inconvenient rather than impossible — this is the difference between an unreported quantity and an unknowable one.

opts.md: The unspecified label boundary of the rule encoder's pre-training
opts.expl: Correct, and the reason is what makes this item different in kind from the other five. Whether the pre-training task used test labels is a fact about the authors' code and data, not about the published model — no re-reading of the paper recovers it, and no experiment by a third party settles it either, because the question is what the original runs did rather than what the method can do. That is why it heads this chapter's list: it is the one item on it that only the authors can close.

A third party can rerun the four constructed datasets at other values of $k$ — the paper reports the construction procedure and the range it chose from, so the experiment is reproducible. The gap is that nobody has run it, not that nobody can.

quiz.q: On Github's production row, GBDT is $85.69$, HGNN is $86.05$, RD-HGNN is $85.93$ and DD-HGNN is $85.96$. What is the best of the paper's two models minus HGNN, to two decimals?
quiz.hint: Take the higher of the two proposed models and subtract the HGNN column. The sign is what matters.
quiz.sol: $85.96 - 86.05 = -0.09$. Table VI prints $+0.00$ in this cell, which converts a near-tie loss into a near-tie win. The magnitude is negligible and the sign is not: it is the difference between a method that beats its own backbone on nine of ten datasets and one that beats it on ten of ten. Neither the abstract nor the conclusion mentions the exception.

quiz.q: You have found one dataset in a paper where the proposed method fails to beat its baseline, and the paper's conclusion claims broad superiority without mentioning it. What is the most useful thing to do next?

opts.expl: Far too strong. A single near-tie — here a 0.09-point deficit — against nine datasets of gains does not refute a method whose mechanism the paper also tests directly. Treating every unmentioned exception as decisive would leave you unable to read any empirical paper.

opts.md: Check whether the exception has a structural explanation, and whether the paper's own framing predicts it
opts.expl: Correct, and this is where an exception earns its keep. Here the paper does state a rule — RD wins on graph datasets, DD on hypergraph datasets — and Github is a graph dataset, so the exception is not random: it is a case where the authors' own account predicts the method should do well. Trying to explain *why* the prediction failed is what turns a 0.09-point curiosity into a question about the method, and it is the same move that turns a limitation into a research direction. **An unexplained exception is a gap; an explained one is a finding.**

opts.md: Check whether the baseline was tuned fairly on that dataset
opts.expl: A reasonable check and a narrower one. It asks whether the comparison is valid, not whether the method's behaviour is understood — and if the baseline turns out to have been tuned fairly, you are back to needing the structural explanation.
